title: Evidence-Based Update on the Surgical Technique and Clinical Outcomes of Retrograde Drilling: A Systematic Review
question: Is the published evidence on retrograde drilling for osteochondral lesions of the talus consistent and strong enough to judge how well the operation works?

bottom_line.question: Is the published evidence on retrograde drilling for osteochondral lesions of the talus consistent and strong enough to judge how well the operation works?
bottom_line.answer: In the studies that used it, the AOFAS foot score rose from 57.9 to 86.1 points after a mean 31.1 months, but the studies were low level, poor quality and inconsistent, so they cannot show how well retrograde drilling works.

sections.title: Talus Lesions and What Retrograde Drilling Is
sections.markdown:
The talus is the bone that forms the lower half of the ankle joint. An **osteochondral lesion of the talus** (OLT) is damage to its surface. That means the cartilage lining the joint, the layer of bone just beneath it (the subchondral bone), or both. These lesions usually follow an ankle injury, and many do not heal on their own. One earlier review found that about half of symptomatic OLTs did not resolve with nonsurgical (conservative) treatment. Surgery gave good-to-excellent results in roughly 85% of patients. Several operations are available, and none has been shown to beat the others.

Retrograde drilling is one of those operations. This systematic review asks how well it has been studied.

## What retrograde drilling is

Many cartilage repairs work from inside the joint and pass through the damaged cartilage. Retrograde drilling comes from the opposite direction. The surgeon drills up into the lesion through the bone and stops short of the cartilage. The procedure is called **non-trans-articular** because the drill never crosses the joint surface. Opening up the damaged bone lets blood vessels grow back in and new bone form, and the cartilage on top, which is often still intact, is left alone. The drilled channel can also be used to pack the lesion with bone graft or a synthetic bone filler.

The technique was first described for the knee in 1981 and applied to the ankle in 1999. A previous review of 80 ankle cases reported success rates of 68% to 90%. Its authors still could not pool the studies statistically because the studies differed too much. That problem is the subject of this review. The authors hypothesized that the literature on retrograde drilling for OLT is **heterogeneous**, meaning the studies vary so much in design and reporting that their results cannot be fairly combined or compared.

sections.title: How the Review Was Done
sections.markdown:
Two foot and ankle surgeons independently searched four medical databases (MEDLINE, Web of Science, EMBASE and the Cochrane Library) for studies published from January 1996 to August 2022. They followed PRISMA, the standard guideline for running and reporting systematic reviews, and a senior author settled disagreements. A study qualified if it reported clinical outcomes of retrograde drilling for OLT in a peer-reviewed, English-language journal. The reviewers excluded animal and lab studies, reviews, case reports, studies with fewer than five patients, and studies with inadequate outcome reporting.

Each study was graded on two scales. The **level of evidence (LoE)** ranks study design, and lower numbers mean stronger designs. Level 4 is typically a case series with no comparison group. The quality of evidence (QoE) was scored with a Modified Coleman Methodology Score. This is a 0 to 100 checklist of methodological features, adapted for cartilage repair in the ankle:

excellent = 85 to 100, good = 70 to 84, fair = 55 to 69, poor = below 55

The reviewers then pulled details from each study:

- patient characteristics
- how lesions were diagnosed, classified and measured, and whether cysts were present
- how the drill was aimed and how wide it was, and whether graft was added
- rehabilitation plans
- clinical scores, imaging results, return to sport and complications

sections.title: What They Found
sections.markdown:
The search turned up 189 studies, and 11 met the criteria. Together they covered 207 ankles.

The evidence base is weak. Two studies were level 3 and nine were level 4, for a mean LoE of 3.8. The mean Coleman score was 50.8 (range 43 to 62). Three studies rated fair and eight rated poor. None reached good or excellent.

Patients averaged 34.4 years old, and 53% were male. Average follow-up was 31.1 months (range 8 to 69), and no study followed patients for more than five years. Studies differed in how long patients tried nonsurgical treatment before surgery, and only six described what that treatment was.

Every study diagnosed lesions with at least two methods. All used plain X-rays, ten used MRI, one used CT, and ten used arthroscopy (a camera inserted into the joint). Nine studies classified the lesions, but they used different systems. Even systems based on the same method (MRI or arthroscopy) did not match. Of the 138 lesions with a reported location, 118 were medial (on the inner side of the talus), 10 were central and 10 were lateral. Only five studies reported lesion size. Nearly all lesions were under 15 mm across or 150 square millimeters in area. Three studies mentioned cysts under the lesion, and none gave the cysts' size.

Surgical technique varied widely. Ten studies inspected the joint with an arthroscope first. All drilled under fluoroscopy (live X-ray), and one added 3D computer-assisted guidance. Five studies used drills 2 mm or thinner, three used 3 to 5 mm, and three used drills wider than 6 mm. Four studies filled the drill holes with the patient's own bone or artificial bone.

Eight studies described their rehabilitation. Most started moving the ankle in the first week. Partial weight-bearing began at 3 to 6 weeks, and every study that gave a date for full weight-bearing chose 6 weeks. Return to full activity was most often set at 6 months.

Ten studies used the **AOFAS score**, a 100-point rating of ankle pain and function from the American Orthopedic Foot and Ankle Society. The weighted average across studies rose from 57.9 before surgery to 86.1 at about 31 months:

improvement = 86.1 - 57.9 = 28.2 points

Eight studies did follow-up MRI. Most described the lesions as improved or healed but gave little detail. Only one study reported return to sport, with all its patients back at 6 months. Nine studies reported complications across 191 ankles: three patients had numbness in the foot and one had a superficial wound infection.

sections.title: What It Means
sections.markdown:
The main finding is the heterogeneity itself. The studies classified lesions differently, used different drills and rehab schedules, and often left out key details. As a result, their findings cannot be pooled or compared directly. With 82% of studies at level 4 and none rated good quality, the authors argue that the standard approach to OLT rests on thin evidence. A 2023 systematic review concluded that retrograde drilling is effective. This review is more cautious because it gives more weight to how poorly the underlying studies were designed and reported.

The authors compare the gaps with 2018 recommendations from the International Consensus Meeting on Cartilage Repair of the Ankle (ICCRA):

- **Nonsurgical care before surgery** was inconsistent. ICCRA recommends 4 to 6 weeks of immobilization with light weight-bearing for acute lesions, with improvement usually seen over 3 to 6 months.
- **Patient selection** was the one area of agreement. Surgeons chose drilling when arthroscopy showed intact cartilage over a lesion in the bone below.
- **Location:** 86% of lesions were medial, compared with 70% to 77% in other reviews. Some surgeons may have drilled only medial lesions, and lateral lesions are more prone to surface-level injury.
- **Lesion size** was rarely reported, although size is the main factor in deciding whether bone marrow stimulation (the family of techniques retrograde drilling belongs to) is suitable. ICCRA recommends bone grafting for lesions more than 1 cm wide or deep and for cysts larger than 100 cubic millimeters. No study measured its cysts.
- **Aiming** is hard. The drill has been reported to miss its target in up to 20% of cases, and fluoroscopy cannot always show the lesion clearly. Navigation systems and MRI guidance exist but are rarely used, and ICCRA considers computer or robot guidance unnecessary. The authors want a simple, accessible way to aim accurately.
- **Drill width** matters because wider holes damage more subchondral bone. That damage may be one reason repaired cartilage wears down over time. A cadaver study found that 1 to 1.25 mm holes did less damage than 2 mm holes, and ICCRA recommends a 1 to 2 mm wire. From their own experience, the authors warn that thin drills can bend or break in the hard bone of young patients.
- **Grafting:** some studies did well with bone graft or synthetic filler and others with drilling alone. None compared the patient's own bone with a synthetic substitute. Synthetic fillers have one advantage: they can flow into irregular, saucer-shaped cysts that are hard to pack with solid bone.

Short-term outcomes were satisfactory. Still, no study went past five years, and follow-up MRI said little about how the subchondral bone changes over time.

sections.title: Limitations and Bottom Line
sections.markdown:
## Limitations

The search ended about a year before publication, which the authors note is typical for systematic reviews. Most included studies were small retrospective case series with short to mid-term follow-up, which carries a high risk of bias. The AOFAS score has never been validated specifically for retrograde drilling of OLT, so it may overstate or understate results. Newer approaches, such as adding stem cells taken from fat tissue or using needle arthroscopy, were outside the review's scope.

## Bottom line

Retrograde drilling for talus lesions appears to improve ankle scores with few complications. The studies behind that impression, though, are small, low in quality and inconsistent in method, so they cannot support firm conclusions or clinical guidelines. The authors call for well-designed clinical trials. These trials should use standard criteria for selecting patients, classifying lesions, performing the surgery and running rehab, and should measure outcomes with validated tools.

anchors.sentence: From their own experience, the authors warn that thin drills can bend or break in the hard bone of young patients.
anchors.quote: In our experience, retrograde drilling performed using a small-diameter drill requires caution, especially in young OLT patients, because the drill may bend or break in the relatively hard bone during the procedure.

anchors.sentence: Grafting:** some studies did well with bone graft or synthetic filler and others with drilling alone.
anchors.quote: In several studies, bone grafting or bone void substitutes were applied through a retrograde approach in lesions, offering satisfactory clinical outcomes,,,, whereas retrograde drilling alone was effective in others.,,,,, Technically, subchondral cysts are filled with bone grafts or bone substitutes via the bone hole made during retrograde drilling.

anchors.sentence: None compared the patient's own bone with a synthetic substitute.
Synthetic fillers have one advantage: they can flow into irregular, saucer-shaped cysts that are hard to pack with solid bone.
anchors.quote: In these cases, bone void substitutes are preferred because they flow to all irregularly shaped defect recesses, thereby eliminating the risk of iatrogenic cartilage damage., To our knowledge, no studies have compared the efficacy of autogenic cancellous bone grafting versus bone void substitutes.

anchors.sentence: Still, no study went past five years, and follow-up MRI said little about how the subchondral bone changes over time.
anchors.quote: As subchondral bone damage is gaining importance in recent research in the field of bone marrow stimulation procedures, changes in the subchondral bone over time after retrograde drilling should be carefully investigated.

anchors.sentence: Retrograde drilling for talus lesions appears to improve ankle scores with few complications.
anchors.quote: The MEDLINE, Web of Science, EMBASE, and Cochrane Library databases were individually searched from January 1996 to August 27, 2022, using the following keywords—“talus” OR “talar” OR “ankle” AND “cartilage” OR “osteochondritis dissecans” OR “chondral” OR “osteochondral” OR “osteochondrolysis” OR “transchondral” OR “osteochondral lesion” OR “OCL” OR “OCD” AND “retrograde drilling.” This search period was chosen based on the findings of a previous systematic review for OLT.

anchors.sentence: The studies behind that impression, though, are small, low in quality and inconsistent in method, so they cannot support firm conclusions or clinical guidelines.

sources.abstract:
Background: Retrograde drilling is an established surgical technique to treat osteochondral lesions of the talus (OLT). It involves non-trans-articular drilling to induce subchondral bone revascularization and bone formation without damaging the overlying articular cartilage. The present study aimed to elucidate the heterogeneity of clinical studies on retrograde drilling for OLT.

Design: A systematic search of the MEDLINE, Web of Science, EMBASE, and Cochrane Library databases for studies published between January 1996 and August 27, 2022, was performed based on the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines by two independent reviewers. The included studies were evaluated for their level of evidence (LoE) and quality of evidence (QoE) using the Modified Coleman Methodology Score. Variables reporting surgical and clinical outcomes and complications were evaluated.

Results: Eleven studies with 207 ankles were included (mean follow-up period = 31.1 months). The mean LoE was 3.8 (LoE 3: two studies, LoE 4: nine studies), and the mean QoE was 50.8 (fair: three studies, poor: eight studies). Ten studies used the American Orthopedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) score, which improved from 57.9 preoperatively to 86.1 postoperatively. The period and protocol of conservative treatment, lesion character, surgical technique, and postoperative protocol were inconsistent or underreported.

Conclusions: This systematic review revealed that low LoE and poor QoE, coupled with heterogeneity among the included studies, impede definitive conclusions regarding the effectiveness of this technique. Consequently, well-designed clinical trials are essential to develop standardized clinical guidelines for using retrograde drilling in OLT.

sources.section5-19476035241239303/p1: Osteochondral lesion of the talus (OLT) is a common cartilage disorder of the ankle, typically resulting from traumatic damage to the articular cartilage and subchondral bone. A systematic review published in 2010 identified that 50% of the primary symptomatic OLTs failed to resolve using conservative treatment, and operative management, including reparative procedures, was most effective with good-to-excellent clinical outcomes in about 85% of the patients. Various surgical techniques, such as bone marrow stimulation, retrograde drilling, osteochondral transplantation, cartilage implantation, and chondrogenesis techniques, are available for treating OLTs; however, it has been reported that none of these techniques was superior to others. Despite the satisfactory outcomes of operative treatment, there are long-term clinical concerns regarding the biological deterioration of the repair.
sources.section5-19476035241239303/p2: Retrograde drilling is a well-known non-trans-articular procedure to induce subchondral bone revascularization and bone formation without disrupting the already damaged talar articular cartilage in OLT. Lee and Mercurioin first described this reparative procedure for knee lesions in 1981, and later, Taranow applied it to the ankle joint in 1999. Eventually, Dahman et al. reported a 68% to 90% success rate of the procedure in a systematic review based on 80 cases of OLT. However, despite the substantial success rates, the authors mentioned that the heterogeneity in the included studies did not allow for pooling. Consequently, homogeneous reporting of outcome data is essential, which allows the pooling and comparison of results to propose and establish clinically relevant guidelines.
sources.section19-19476035241239303/p2: We observed that there were significant inconsistencies in the existing literature regarding the modalities and period of conservative treatment for OLTs. Although most studies have described the period of conservative treatment, the duration was variable. Furthermore, the detailed protocol was not described appropriately in any of the studies reviewed. Currently, various conservative treatment options for OLT are available, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or acetaminophen, rest and activity restriction, and cast immobilization. Since the evidence regarding the best conservative treatment for OLTs remains contentious, in 2018, the International Consensus Meeting on Cartilage Repair of the Ankle (ICCRA) published consensus statements. They stated thatthe optimal protocol for conservative management of an acute nondisplaced osteochondral lesion of the ankle is immobilization for 4–6 weeks with touchdown weight-bearing. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can be prescribed in cases of significant pain and swelling unless otherwise medically contraindicated
